papers.title: Antibiotics drive immunometabolic rewiring of human immune responses
papers.abstract: Antibiotics are routinely evaluated for their antimicrobial activity, potential host toxicity, and disruption of the microbiome. Certain antibiotics can also impact cell-intrinsic host processes, including evolutionarily conserved processes in the mitochondria. These raise the possibility that antibiotics can directly impact host immunity, which relies on mitochondrial function for their immunometabolic activation. However, the immunological consequences of most antibiotics in current use have not been systematically examined. Here, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the effects of clinically used antibiotics on activation of primary human immune cells. We uncovered an underappreciated antibiotic-specific modulation of immune function in healthy individuals and infectious disease patients. Focusing on the immunomodulatory antibiotic ciprofloxacin, we found altered mitochondrial gene expression across multiple immune populations, driving distinct, lineage-specific responses and heightened sensitivity of T-cells. Ciprofloxacin impaired primary human T-cell expansion and activation and altered mitochondrial function and metabolism. We further demonstrated immunomodulatory effects of selected antibiotics in response to inactivated bacteria and during live viral infection. Finally, to test the implications of our findings in vivo, we showed that immune activation is altered shortly after a single dose of antibiotic administration in mice. This work established a widespread impact of antibiotics on immune-cell function, and identified mitochondrial perturbation as one underlying mechanism, with implications for host-pathogen interactions and antimicrobial therapy.

papers.title: CTLA-4 checkpoint signalling modulates germinal centre dynamics and antibody avidity during Borrelia burgdorferi infection in mice.
papers.abstract: Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme borreliosis, persists in mammalian hosts despite robust activation of innate and adaptive immunity. A hallmark of murine infection is the production of low-avidity antibodies, yet the immunological mechanisms underlying this defective humoral response remain poorly understood. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing of draining lymph node cells from Borrelia-infected mice at days 7 and 14 post-infection, comparing transcriptional profiles with those from mice immunised with heat-killed Borrelia or with a potent germinal centre-inducing protein immunisation. Borrelia infection induced a rapid germinal centre response, however, light zone B cells displayed diminished expression of co-stimulatory and T-B cell interaction molecules while maintaining core germinal centre identity markers, suggesting impaired positive selection. T follicular helper cells upregulated multiple inhibitory checkpoint receptor genes, most prominently Ctla4, alongside an active germinal centre engagement programme. Foxp3? regulatory T cells upregulated genes associated with follicular-homing and suppressive function, including those implicated in CTLA-4-mediated trans-endocytosis. To test whether inhibitory signalling contributes to the impaired humoral response, infected mice were treated with anti-CTLA-4 blocking antibody. CTLA-4 blockade significantly increased plasma cell numbers and enhanced both the magnitude and avidity of Borrelia-specific IgG responses, including the induction of complement-fixing IgG2a. These findings reveal that CTLA-4-dependent inhibitory signalling contributes to defective antibody quality during Borrelia infection, identifying a mechanism by which dysregulated T cell responses may facilitate impaired humoral control of a persistent spirochaetal pathogen.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Analysis of Innate Immune Responses to Toxoplasma gondii in Bat Cells
papers.abstract: Bats exhibit remarkable tolerance to numerous viral infections, a phenotype associated with distinctive adaptations in innate immune and inflammatory pathways. Whether these adaptations also shape responses to nonviral intracellular pathogens remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the interaction between the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii and epithelial cell lines derived from the black flying fox (Pteropus alecto). We found that both type I and type II strains of T. gondii readily invaded and replicated in bat cells, demonstrating a high degree of cellular permissiveness to infection. Surprisingly, transcriptomic analysis revealed remarkably limited early host responses despite progressive intracellular parasite replication. A pronounced transcriptional response emerged only at later stages of infection, coinciding with extensive parasite replication and cellular damage, and was characterized by changes in genes associated with inflammatory signaling, metabolic adaptation, and tissue remodeling. Together, these findings reveal an unusual interaction between bat cells and an intracellular protozoan pathogen, characterized by efficient parasite replication and markedly delayed host transcriptional activation. Our results suggest that distinctive regulation of cellular responses to intracellular infection may extend beyond viral pathogens and represent a broader feature of bat immune biology.

papers.title: Inherited maternal memory T cells protect offspring from respiratory viral infection through disease tolerance
papers.abstract: Maternal immune transfer is a powerful mechanism for early-life protection from infection, yet the full repertoire of protective factors remains unknown. We discovered that maternal memory T cells are both necessary and sufficient to protect offspring from lethal respiratory infection. This antigen-specific protection operated independently of maternal antibodies and offspring T cell responses and required IL-10 produced by maternal T cells. Transfer of protective maternal T cells reduced offspring inflammatory responses and lung tissue damage without affecting viral burdens, indicating that maternal memory T cells directly suppress pathogenic innate inflammatory responses to preserve offspring health. Critically, maternal vaccination similarly protected offspring in a T cell-dependent manner. These findings reveal maternal antigen-specific T cell transfer as a complementary immunological defense mechanism to protect offspring against pathogens that escape maternal antibodies, with broad implications for maternal vaccination strategies.

papers.title: HLAResolver: A statistical framework for resolving HLA ambiguity in T-cell response data
papers.abstract: Large-scale models of T-cell recognition require training examples that specify the complete T-cell receptor (TCR)-peptide-human leukocyte antigen (HLA) complex. Multiplexed Identification of T-cell Receptor Antigen Specificity (MIRA) is a high-throughput assay that identifies TCRs associated with responses to specific peptides, but does not determine which HLA presents each peptide. Because a donor can carry up to six distinct class I HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C alleles, each response may have several candidate presenting HLAs. To narrow this set of candidate presenting HLAs, we developed HLAResolver, a statistical framework that combines MIRA response patterns across HLA-typed donors with NetMHCpan predictions of peptide presentation. For each peptide, HLAResolver uses negative-binomial regression to jointly estimate associations between HLA alleles and TCR response counts, accounting for differences in assay yield. NetMHCpan eluted-ligand predictions guide sparse regularization, favoring alleles with stronger predicted presentation while allowing strong MIRA response evidence to support alternatives. To assess whether this integration provides an advantage over either approach alone, we compared HLAResolver with NetMHCpan, which predicts peptide-HLA presentation, and the Restrictor Analysis Tool for Epitopes (RATE), which infers HLA associations from T-cell response patterns. Using held-out MIRA experiments, we assessed each method's ability to predict observed responses and the number of candidate HLAs it assigned. At matched specificity for predicting MIRA responses, HLAResolver achieved higher sensitivity while selecting fewer candidate HLAs per peptide than either comparator.

papers.title: Protection against disseminated disease following reinfection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis requires CD8+ lymphocytes
papers.abstract: Concomitant immunity is protective adaptive immunity conferred by pre-existing infection against subsequent exposures. This phenomenon is effective in the context of human tuberculosis (TB) and has been successfully recapitulated in non-human primates (NHPs). We previously demonstrated that depletion of CD4 T cells prior to secondary challenge with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) only partially abrogated protection, implicating a critical role for additional cell types. Here, we describe the effects of depleting CD8 expressing cells in this model. CD4+ T cells in the airway were unable to compensate for lost cytotoxicity due to CD8 depletion. Contrary to the results of CD4 depletion, CD8 depleted animals exhibited a unique inability to limit Mtb dissemination, with significant lymph node involvement despite a short 4-week infection. These data suggest that concomitant immunity relies on non-redundant roles played by CD8+ lymphocytes. Thus, future vaccines should be designed to induce effective responses by both CD4+ and CD8+ populations to maximize efficacy.

papers.title: Serial intravascular labeling resolves dynamic decidual NK residency and gestational remodeling toward T-bet-Low states
papers.abstract: Decidual natural killer (dNK) cells are the predominant immune population at the maternal-fetal interface during early pregnancy. However, how vascular trafficking, tissue residency, proliferation, and apoptosis-associated activity are coordinated to establish and maintain the dNK population throughout pregnancy remains unclear. We hypothesized that gestational remodeling of the dNK compartment reflects coordinated changes in these cellular processes in association with progressive T-bet downregulation. We combined serial intravascular labeling (SIVL), flow cytometry, BrdU incorporation, active caspase-3 detection, spatial imaging, and Tbx21 fate mapping to examine NK cells in virgin mice and across gestation. Pregnancy altered CD49a/CD49b-defined dNK-cell composition and redistributed dNK cells among SIVL-defined vascular-accessibility states, supporting a model of dynamic dNK-cell tissue residency. Trafficking-associated marker scores displayed continuous gradients of tissue retention, circulatory/egress potential, and chemokine responsiveness rather than defining a single resident state. Spatial imaging demonstrated greater dNK-cell density in the mesometrial decidua and preferential CD31 vessel contact by recently intravascular dNK cells during early and mid-gestation. BrdU incorporation and active caspase-3 positivity peaked during early pregnancy and varied across SIVL-defined states. Tbx21 fate mapping identified a progressive and selective shift from current T-bet expression toward ex-T-bet and non-fate-mapped Eomes dNK states. T-bet-low states preferentially maintained proliferation at mid-gestation, whereas current T-bet expression was associated with greater circulatory/egress potential. However, active caspase-3 was not selectively increased in current T-bet-expressing cells. Collectively, these findings identify pregnancy-induced dNK-cell remodeling as a coordinated process integrating dynamic tissue residency, vascular accessibility, local proliferation, and apoptosis-associated activity, alongside a progressive shift toward T-bet-low dNK states.

papers.title: Serotype specific anti-capsular polysaccharide IgG associated with colonizing and invasive group B streptococcus in pregnant woman-newborn dyads
papers.abstract: Maternal IgG against group B streptococcus (GBS) capsular polysaccharide (CPS), is the principal placental mediator of neonatal protection, yet naturally acquired anti-CPS immunity has not been characterized in North African populations. To address this gap, we conducted a prospective study in a Moroccan mother-newborn cohort to quantify the serotype-specific anti-CPS IgG levels in relation to colonizing versus invasive GBS serotypes. Additionally, we assessed the transplacental transfer of anti-CPS IgG and identified potential correlates of invasive disease. We examined serotype-specific anti-CPS IgG (serotypes Ia-V) in the plasma from maternal and cord blood of 103 GBS-colonized pregnant women, 35 uncolonized controls and their paired newborns (90 paired colonized dyads, including five newborns with invasive GBS disease) using a standardized six-plex immunoassay. Transfer ratios were compared with 1.0 and cord concentrations with published serotype- and onset-specific risk-reduction thresholds. Maternal anti-CPS IgG concentrations varied by serotype, with the highest median for serotype II(1.36g/mL) and the lowest for serotype Ib(0.003g/mL). They were higher in GBS-colonized than uncolonized mothers for serotypes Ia, Ib and II. Maternal and cord blood IgG concentrations were correlated across serotypes, but placental transfer was incomplete, with median ratios of 0.50-0.80. Among 77 newborns, 13.0%(n=10) reached early-onset and 44.2%(n=34) achieved late-onset disease risk-reduction thresholds. The serotype IV was the most identified among neonatal infection disease cases, and this was associated with sub-protective anti-serotype IV antibody. This suggests that while naturally acquired anti-serotype II antibodies were predominant, the low level of anti-serotype IV antibodies could contribute to neonatal infection diseases in mother-newborn pairs.

papers.title: Identification of Cryptococcus neoformans capsule-associated protein antigens that mediate B cell-dependent vaccine protection in mice and elicit antibody responses in humans with cryptococcosis
papers.abstract: Infection with the encapsulated fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans causes substantial global disease burden in persons with compromised T cell function. Previously, we demonstrated that vaccines containing adjuvanted recombinant cryptococcal proteins protected mice against lethal infection by mechanisms dependent on CD4+ T cells. For the present study, we hypothesized that vaccines containing protein antigens naturally located on the surface of the cryptococcal capsule would contribute protective B cell responses. We found that B cell-deficient mice exhibited reduced survival following vaccination with any of four capsule-associated antigens: Blp4, Cpd1, Lhc1, or Krp1. To further elucidate the role of antibodies in protection, we tested serum from mice vaccinated with a live-attenuated strain (cda123) and then challenged with a virulent C. neoformans strain for IgG responses to a panel of 26 cryptococcal recombinant proteins. Strong reactivity was detected against Blp4, which we focused on because it is capsule-associated and protects mice when administered in adjuvanted subunit vaccines, by mechanisms partly dependent on B cells. Blp4 antibodies were consistently present in surviving mice, including those vaccinated with unrelated proteins or those challenged with diverse clinical isolates. Additionally, serum from Blp4-vaccinated mice promoted macrophage opsonophagocytosis of C. neoformans. Finally, IgG antibodies against Blp4 were detected in 20 of 21 serum samples from patients who survived cryptococcosis, compared with only 4 of 14 samples from healthy controls. Together, these data identify Blp4 as an antigen that elicits protective B cell responses and is a strong candidate for inclusion in subunit cryptococcal vaccines.

papers.title: Genetically restricted human antibodies recognize a conserved β-hairpin in postfusion influenza hemagglutinin
papers.abstract: A public class of broadly protective, human antibodies (Abs) binds a conserved {beta}-hairpin exposed in the postfusion conformation of influenza virus hemagglutinin (HA). We here describe use of in vitro immunoassays and high-resolution cryogenic electron microscopy analysis of Ab:HA complexes to explain the apparent genetic restriction of these Abs and the wide range of influenza A and B subtypes they recognize. We show that recognition of the {beta}-hairpin epitope requires 1) germline-encoded residues unique to certain alleles of the human immunoglobulin heavy chain gene IGHV1-2, 2) a short ( 75% of people have the necessary IGHV1-2 alleles to make these Abs. We conclude that an immunogen that displays the {beta}-hairpin epitope might reliably elicit broadly protective influenza antibodies in most humans.

papers.title: Anti-TGFβ peptide P144 augments CAR-T cell efficacy through neutrophil recruitment and TME remodeling in malignant mesothelioma
papers.abstract: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare, aggressive and highly desmoplastic cancer characterised by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, but its activity against solid tumours such as mesothelioma remains limited, in part through transforming growth factor-beta (TGF{beta})-mediated immunosuppression. To address this barrier, we engineered murine CAR-T cells that simultaneously target tumour antigen and deliver TGF{beta} blockade to the tumour. We first compared two anti-TGF{beta} peptides, the beta glycan-derived P144 and the phage-display-derived P17, in vitro; both attenuated TGF{beta}-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and reporter activity, but P144 suppressed canonical Smad3 phosphorylation more effectively and was selected for downstream work. Murine CAR constructs targeting either mesothelin (M11) or fibroblast activation protein (FAP) were modified to secrete P144, and the resulting products were assessed in co-culture assays and in the syngeneic AE17m model of mesothelioma. P144 secretion did not alter transduction efficiency, expansion or antigen-specific cytotoxicity, but markedly increased antigen-driven IFN{gamma} production, most notably at low effector-to-target ratios. In vivo, both M11-P144 and FAP-P144 CAR-T cells-controlled tumour growth better than their parental, peptide-free counterparts, although complete tumour resolution was not achieved. Flow cytometric profiling of the tumour immune infiltrate showed that P144 delivery increased intratumoral neutrophil frequency approximately three-fold, and neutrophils recovered from these tumours were substantially more cytotoxic ex vivo than those from control tumours. Antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion attenuated the additional benefit conferred by P144 while leaving parental CAR-T activity largely intact, indicating that neutrophils contribute functionally to the effect. Local, CAR-T-delivered TGF{beta} blockade therefore remodels the mesothelioma TME and engages a tumoricidal neutrophil response, offering a modular strategy for enhancing adoptive cell therapy in desmoplastic solid tumours.

papers.title: The IFN-γ-inducible GTPase IIGP1 regulates mitochondrial remodeling and immunometabolic reprogramming during inflammatory macrophage polarization
papers.abstract: Macrophages are key effector cells of the innate immune system that undergo dynamic polarization into functionally distinct phenotypic states, ranging from classically activated inflammatory (M1) to alternatively activated (M2) macrophages. Inflammatory macrophage polarization requires coordinated integration of cytokine signaling, metabolic reprogramming, and mitochondrial remodeling. However, the molecular effectors that control inflammatory signaling for mitochondrial metabolism and remodeling remain poorly defined. Using quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics, we identified Interferon-inducible GTPase 1 (IIGP1) as one of the most robustly induced proteins during inflammatory macrophage polarization. Its expression is governed by the IFN-{gamma}-JAK-STAT1 signaling axis and is crucial for this polarization process. IIGP1-deficient macrophages exhibited significantly impaired iNOS induction, nitric oxide production, pro-inflammatory gene expression, co-stimulatory surface marker expression, and morphological remodeling. Further, IIGP1 associates with mitochondria and its absence impairs key characteristics of inflammatory macrophages, including glycolytic metabolic reprogramming, mitochondrial redox adaptation, membrane potential regulation, and structural remodeling. Consistent with these defects, IIGP1-deficient macrophages displayed impaired intracellular killing of Escherichia coli and Salmonella Typhimurium. Collectively, these results point to IIGP1 as an IFN-{gamma}-inducible effector that facilitates efficient inflammatory macrophage polarization and antibacterial immunity by linking inflammatory signaling to mitochondrial homeostasis and immunometabolic reprogramming.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics of pediatric tuberculosis lymph nodes reveals a conserved hypoxia_SPP1 niche
papers.abstract: Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) often presents as primary disease involving the mediastinal lymph nodes; however, its granuloma microenvironment remains poorly characterized because these population patient tissues are rarely available for study. Here, we use spatial transcriptomics to profile 60 granulomas from four children aged 4 to 36 months. We identified nine recurrent transcriptional microenvironments shared across granulomas, despite their marked histological heterogeneity. One macrophage-rich microenvironment showed strong hypoxia-associated activity and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) enrichment. This microenvironment was present in both non-necrotic and necrotic lesions and overlapped with a Mtb-persistence macrophage signature previously identified in murine TB lymph nodes. Pathway analysis revealed the enrichment of both antimicrobial and regulatory programs within this microenvironment, suggesting partial immune control rather than uniform inflammatory or suppressive activity in this region. SPP1 expression was associated with regions enriched for both M1- and M2-like macrophages, suggesting a macrophage program that extends beyond conventional polarization classifications and may be influenced by the local granuloma microenvironment. We further observed a similar spatial association between hypoxia-associated activity and SPP1 expression in an independent adult TB dataset (pooled Spearman {rho}=0.65) and validated this association at protein level by multiplex immunofluorescence in our pediatric TB granuloma sample. Overall, this study identified a hypoxia-associated SPP1-enriched microenvironment that may contribute to incomplete bacterial clearance and could provide a framework for evaluating host-directed strategies to enhance sterilizing immunity without exacerbating tissue damage.

papers.title: Enzymatic attachment of antigens to probe immune modulation by skin commensals
papers.abstract: The skin colonist Staphylococcus epidermidis induces potent T and B cell responses, which can be redirected against antigens of interest by genetic engineering. However, since many taxa in the microbiome are genetically intractable, the utility of this method is limited. Here, we use recombinant sortase to conjugate antigens to the surface of a wide range of Gram-positive bacterial species, and we show that this non-genetic method can be used to generate protective immunity in vivo.

papers.title: A Reproducible Pre-Transplant γδ T-cell Effector Signature Reveals Immune-Metabolic Programs Associated with Kidney Allograft Rejection
papers.abstract: Despite optimized immunosuppression, acute kidney transplant rejection affects 10-20% of recipients within the first year, and no reliable pre-transplant molecular test exists to identify patients at high risk, independent of the donor HLA matching. Across three independent cohorts of kidney transplant recipients, profiled by bulk RNA-sequencing with T-cell receptor repertoire analysis, flow cytometry, CyTOF with paired metabolomics, we identified a reproducible depletion of {gamma}{delta} T cells associated with rejection: an elevated {beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell ratio in two post-transplant, biopsy-matched cohorts, and depletion of specific {gamma}{delta} T effector clusters in a third, longitudinally sampled cohort. In this third cohort, {gamma}{delta} T cell depletion was already present at the pre-transplant baseline in patients who subsequently developed rejection and remained detectable across the transplant course, indicating that it reflects recipient baseline immune biology rather than a consequence of graft injury. Longitudinal metabolomic profiling in this cohort identified time-dependent metabolic changes, including in amino acid metabolism that co-occur with the {gamma}{delta} signature and converge with it upon multi-omics integration. At the pre-transplant baseline, {gamma}{delta} T-cell marker expression alone showed exploratory discriminatory value for rejection risk (AUC = 0.69), improving marginally when integrated with metabolomic features (AUC = 0.71); larger prospective studies will be needed before clinical translation.

papers.title: Decoding antibody-antigen recognition: the BL8 language and its application in calibrating deep learning predictions
papers.abstract: Antibodies are central to immunology and therapeutics, and understanding how they recognize antigens is essential to rational drug design. This recognition depends on the interplay of interface geometry, physicochemical interactions, sequence context, and complementarity-determining region (CDR) conformation. However, traditional analyses often oversimplify this complexity, which becomes particularly problematic when evaluating the massive and frequently overconfident structural hypotheses generated by modern deep learning models. Here, we introduce BL8, an interpretable, eight-view structural language that comprehensively parameterizes interfaces across topology, shape, interaction, CDR conformation, flexibility, interfacial area, amino-acid-pair composition, and sequence background. Using 15,396 experimental interface records from the Structural Antibody Database (SAbDab), we built a fixed reference atlas containing 1,498 discrete BL8 signatures. The atlas shows that natural interfaces occupy a diverse, long-tailed structural space in which similar geometric scaffolds can be associated with different chemical and sequence features. Furthermore, we projected 28,501 predicted complexes involving programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD), and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), generated using AlphaFold 3 (AF3), Protenix-v2, and OpenDDE, into the reference space. Acting as a robust underlying calibration layer, BL8 successfully decoupled physical viability from native confidence illusions, revealing cross-target hallucinations and filtering out 15.3% to 20.1% of highly deceptive false-positive predictions. Crucially, by benchmarking distinct generative behaviors across models, it enabled the extraction of highly reliable, multi-model consensus out-of-distribution binding paradigms. Together, BL8 bridges foundational biophysics with large-scale computational predictions, providing an essential benchmarking framework for discovering novel mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Immuno-Proteomic Age of Cardiovascular Etiology (iPACE) Signature Predicts Cardiovascular Risk in Elderly Patients
papers.abstract: Despite advances in clinical care, cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of disability and mortality worldwide. While age alone is a primary risk factor for CVD, accumulating evidence suggests the immune system influences the initiation and progression of CVD pathophysiology, particularly in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD). Here, using two independent cohorts of older adults, we develop a thirty-protein signature of age based on serum immune proteomics, which correlates with HFpEF and ASCVD risk and mortality (Immuno-Proteomic Age of Cardiovascular Etiology, iPACE). We find aging-related circulating immune proteins associated with ASCVD and HFpEF-specific resilience and susceptibility that may be used as potential prognostic, diagnostic, or therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Foreign Body Responses Adapt to Systemic Immunosuppression to Maintain Local Immune Homeostasis Through Decorin-Associated Signaling
papers.abstract: Foreign body responses (FBRs) involve complex interactions between pro- and anti-inflammatory signals that regulate the integration and function of implanted biomaterials. However, most mechanistic studies of FBRs have been conducted in healthy hosts, and little is known about how these immune responses are regulated under pathological conditions. Here, we investigated immune responses to porous polycaprolactone (PCL) scaffold implants in mice with endotoxin tolerance or aggressive breast tumors, which induce systemic immunosuppression through distinct mechanisms. Despite suppressed inflammatory activity in major organs, implanted scaffolds maintained locally immune-active environments characterized by increased pro-inflammatory immune-cell populations and elevated inflammatory mediators, including CXCL1. In migration assays, CXCL1 preferentially recruited neutrophils and enriched immune-cell populations with pro-inflammatory phenotypes among splenocytes derived from both endotoxin-tolerant and tumor-bearing mice. The extracellular matrix proteoglycan decorin, a damage-associated molecular pattern with TLR2/4-activating activity in myeloid cells, was enriched within scaffolds but reduced in major organs under both immunosuppressive conditions. Recombinant decorin promoted pro-inflammatory phenotypes in suppressive myeloid-cell populations and enhanced CXCL1 production through TLR2/4-associated signaling, suggesting a mechanistic link between decorin-mediated myeloid activation, CXCL1-dependent immune-cell recruitment, and the maintenance of local immune activity at biomaterial interfaces. Together, these findings reveal that FBRs are not merely passive inflammatory reactions to biomaterial implants but can dynamically adapt to systemic immune dysfunction to sustain local immune homeostasis. This intrinsic immunoregulatory capacity may represent an additional factor influencing the performance of immunomodulatory implants and should be considered in biomaterial design to optimize therapeutic outcomes across different applications and host immune conditions.

papers.title: TREM2 encodes plaque macrophage plasticity to mediate atherosclerosis regression
papers.abstract: Cholesterol lowering therapies stabilize atherosclerotic plaque and reduce ischemic events, but the molecular mechanisms governing plaque remodeling or regression remain poorly defined. The lipid sensor TREM2 is a key modulator of plaque-associated foam cell development and was upregulated by plaque macrophages in atherosclerosis regression. We examined macrophage- or monocyte-specific Trem2 deletion during regression in mice and found that TREM2 expression on plaque macrophages, not newly recruited monocytes, was required for plaque regression. Trem2 deletion impeded necrotic core resolution, leading us to interrogate the efferocytic capacity of TREM2+ cells during lipid lowering. An in vitro model of cholesterol-experienced ex-lipid associated macrophages (Ex-LAMs) demonstrated that prior lipid priming enhanced efferocytic ability after unloading lipids and maintained expression of lysosomal and cytoskeletal remodeling genes. Augmented TREM2 signaling through genetic models or agonist treatment accelerated efferocytic ability in vitro and plaque regression in vivo. Thus, we posit that a TREM2-dependent ExLAM programming drives atherosclerosis resolution and facilitates beneficial plaque remodeling through enhanced efferocytosis. Overall, targeting the TREM2 pathway may be a viable strategy for stabilizing atherosclerotic plaques in patients treated with aggressive cholesterol control.

papers.title: Gene regulatory logic underlying the differentiation of mixed lineages in human thymic epithelial cells
papers.abstract: The thymus enacts central tolerance through thymic (TECs), which present self-antigens to developing T cells self-reactive cells, preventing autoimmunity. Human TECs include populations that express lineage-committed programs corresponding to distinct peripheral tissues, yet how they acquire these programs and whether these TEC subpopulations are genetically related and conserved in mice remain unknown. Using matched single-cell gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiling of 126,687 human TECs, we identified 17 TEC subsets defined by their distinct expression profiles of 1,843 cell type restricted-antigens (CRAs) from 48 peripheral cell types. With a new phylogenetic reconstruction method, we show that lineage-committed TECs share a common ancestor, retain a thymus-specific mixed identity through co-expression of multiple CRA signatures, and are specified by coordinated activator and repressor regulons. We also identified a basement-membrane-collagen-rich state (BMC-TECs) with progenitor-like properties. Finally, mouse TECs shared the regulatory strategy but conserved few master transcription-factor drivers. This study mechanistically characterizes human TEC subpopulations and reveals the gene regulatory logic that leads to their distinct diversification and mixed identities in humans and mice.

papers.title: A minimal two-residue C-terminal truncation of AID in adult-onset hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2)
papers.abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), encoded by AICDA, facilitates class-switch recombination (CSR) and somatic hypermutation (SHM) in activated B cells. Loss of AID function causes hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2). While typically autosomal recessive, three C-terminal truncation variants have been reported to act in autosomal dominant manner. We describe a novel heterozygous AICDA nonsense variant, c.589G>T (p.G197*), that truncates the final two C-terminal residues of AID and results in adult-onset HIGM2. Single-cell sequencing of primary patient B cells revealed a complete block in CSR and a [~]10-fold reduction in SHM. AICDA mRNA expression was balanced between wild-type and variant alleles, yet AID protein abundance was reduced to [~]56% with normal subcellular localization. Remarkably, inducible germinal center (iGB) cultures restored CSR in purified naive patient B cells. CRISPR-Cas9 editing of healthy donor B cells confirmed that the iGB platform can rescue B cells harboring heterozygous, but not homozygous, AICDA variants. These results demonstrate that even a two-amino-acid truncation at the AID C-terminus is sufficient to disrupt its function and cause HIGM2.

papers.title: Caspase-1 and -11 defend against environmental but not host-adapted pathogens in genetically complex mice
papers.abstract: Caspase-1 and -11 are inflammatory caspases that trigger pyroptosis, yet in most infection models they confer only a modest survival benefit. We have proposed that caspase-1 and -11 evolved primarily to defend against ubiquitous environmental microbes that have not been under selective pressure to evade them, whereas host-adapted pathogens have evolved evasion strategies. Testing this idea is complicated because the inbred mouse strains used in most infection studies carry mutations in innate immune genes: i.e., C57BL/6 (B6) mice carry a loss-of-function Nramp1 allele, and 129 mice lack functional caspase-11. Here we generated B6 x 129 F1 hybrid mice, which are gene-sufficient at both Nramp1 and Casp11, and used them to measure the fold change in lethal dose ({triangleup}LD100) caused by caspase-1 and -11 deficiency for four pathogens on the B6, 129, and F1 backgrounds. Caspase-1 and -11 conferred little or no survival benefit against the host-adapted pathogens Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella Typhimurium on any of the three backgrounds, apart from a modest benefit at the lowest S. Typhimurium inoculum in F1 mice. In contrast, caspase-1 and -11 were required to survive infection with the environmental pathogens Burkholderia thailandensis and Chromobacterium violaceum, where caspase-1 and -11 deficiency lowered the lethal dose by up to six orders of magnitude. The failure of caspase-1 and -11 against host-adapted pathogens therefore persists on a genetically robust hybrid background, supporting the view that a major evolutionary role of caspase-1 and -11 is defense against environmental microbes that have not been selected to evade them.

papers.title: Induced microfold cells are required for the function of pulmonary tertiary lymphoid organs that promote mucosal immunity
papers.abstract: Tertiary lymphoid organs (TLOs) arise in response to infection and inflammation. We show that influenza-induced lung TLOs are comprised of inducible M cell (iM cell)-inducible bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (iBALT) functional composites. iM cells are necessary for the appropriate architecture of adjacent immune follicles, which contain clonally expanded and sequence-diversified B cells. iM cell ablation results in fewer antigen-specific germinal center B cells, T follicular helper cells, and T helper memory cells, and a decrease in secretory IgA and IgG production accompanied by a loss of viral control. We find that the iM cells arise from epithelial progenitors that respond to a RANKL signal from infiltrating T cells, consistent with a model in which the patchy inflammation typical of pneumonia results in the unpredictable and varying distribution of coupled iM cells and adjacent iBALT. We propose that iM cells could be harnessed to promote infection control and enhance mucosal vaccination.

papers.title: Defining the Functional Consequence of the Human Ocular Microbiome
papers.abstract: The ocular surface is one of the body's most environmentally exposed mucosal barriers, yet it is considered low biomass and harbors orders of magnitude fewer bacteria than microbe-rich sites like the gut. This has cast doubt on whether a functional core ocular microbiome exists at all. Having previously defined a protective gd T cell and IL-17 axis engaged by the murine commensal Corynebacterium mastitidis, we asked whether human-derived bacteria could do the same. Pairing sequencing and culturomics of healthy human conjunctiva from two geographically distinct cohorts, we define a stable core microbiome and identify Corynebacterium bovis as a consistent eye-resident commensal rather than a transient contaminant. In humans, C. bovis elicits a non-pathogenic response marked by IL-17 secretion by {gamma}{delta} T cells and circulating C. bovis-specific IgG, which suggests commensalism rather than pathology. Colonizing mice with human C. bovis strains from Pittsburgh or Miami reproduced this program and conferred protection against ocular infection with Staphylococcus aureus. Together, these findings identify C. bovis as a human-derived ocular commensal that can drive protective {gamma}{delta} T cell immunity, translating a mechanism previously defined only in mice into human relevance and a rational target against sight-threatening infection.

papers.title: JAK1/2 Inhibition Restores Tissue Integrity by Rewiring Type 1/2 Immunity Toward Targetable IL-17 Responses
papers.abstract: Effective immune responses require coordinated communication between immune and epithelial cells to eliminate pathogens while limiting tissue damage. Disruption of this balance drives chronic inflammation and progressive tissue destruction. The Janus kinase (JAK) pathway coordinates cytokine signaling across these compartments and has emerged as a therapeutic target in inflammatory diseases. However, the consequences of JAK inhibition within a complex inflammatory environment remain incompletely understood. Here, we dissect the molecular, cellular, immunological and phenotypical effects of topical JAK1/2 inhibition in a chronic model of tissue-destructive skin inflammation driven by barrier dysfunction and bacterial superinfection. Single-cell transcriptomics and functional profiling revealed that JAK1/2 blockade selectively suppressed pathogenic CD8 T cells and their IFN-{gamma} production while shifting Th2-polarized CD4 T cells toward a Th17 phenotype, preserving type 3 immunity consisting of IL-17A-producing {gamma}{delta}-T cells and neutrophil responses. This immune rebalancing occurs rapidly and concomitantly with the restoration of epithelial barrier integrity through tight junction reinforcement, followed by recovery of antimicrobial defenses and reduced bacterial burden. Combination of JAK1/2 and IL-17A blockade further improved tissue homeostasis by targeting residual type 3-driven pathology. Thus, JAK1/2 inhibition acts as selective immunomodulator rather than a broad immunosuppressant, targeting pathogenic type 1/2 responses while preserving type-3-associated antimicrobial defense programs. These findings reveal how JAK1/2 inhibition coordinates immune rebalancing with epithelial repair and support its therapeutic potential in chronic type 1/2-driven inflammatory disease, while identifying residual IL-17A-mediated pathology as a target for combination therapy.

papers.title: CD19-CAR T-cell therapy resets the EBV+ autoreactive B cell repertoire in autoimmune disease
papers.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reprograms autoreactive B cells into activated antigen-presenting cells that drive pathogenic T- and B-cell responses in autoimmune disease. Whether eliminating these cells contributes to durable remission after CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy is unknown. Here, using EBV B-cell sequencing (EBV-seq), we profiled EBV+ B cells from patients treated with CD19-CAR T cells (systemic lupus erythematosus, n=6; inflammatory myopathy, n=3; systemic sclerosis, n=3) or rituximab (n=15) and recombinantly expressed their antibodies to define antigen specificity. At baseline, EBV+ B cells were enriched relative to healthy donors, class-switched and hypermutated, expressed the latency III program with heightened antigen-presentation signatures, and encoded autoantibodies. CAR T cells, but not rituximab, depleted EBV+ B cells and shifted the reconstituted repertoire towards IgM+, minimally mutated, largely non-autoreactive cells, consistent with infection of newly generated B cells. After rituximab, EBV+ B cells retained a class-switched, hypermutated and autoreactive with an activated antigen-presenting phenotype. Sustained drug-free remission occurred in 8/12 CAR T-cell-treated versus 0/15 rituximab-treated patients. In vitro, EBV+ B cells resisted anti-CD20 and anti-CD19 antibodies but were killed by CAR T cells and a CD19 T-cell engager. Our findings suggest resetting the EBV+ autoreactive B-cell repertoire contributes to sustained drug-free remission.

papers.title: A network of bZIP transcription factors and inhibitors enforces differentially proliferative and cytotoxic states in T cells
papers.abstract: The bZIP family of transcription factors (TFs) plays a central role in regulating T-cell exhaustion. Their complex dimeric interactions obscure the roles of individual members, which genetic knockout or overexpression alone poorly resolve. Here, we use overexpression of full-length bZIP family TFs alongside genetically encoded, protein-based inhibitors to probe the effect of increased or decreased bZIP TF activity on CAR T-cell expansion under exhausting conditions. Enrichment of inhibitors of pro-exhaustion TFs (CREM, NFIL3) illustrated the utility of this approach. The screen enriched full-length TFs of established anti-exhaustion relevance and identified underappreciated bZIP TFs such as BATF2. Detailed comparison of several bZIP TFs and inhibitors revealed distinct effects on proliferation, persistence, and cytotoxicity. We investigated combinations of pro-cytotoxic JUN, pro-proliferative BATF2, and a novel inhibitor (AEL-CREM) of pro-dysfunction CREM. Distinct pairs were more advantageous for maintenance of cytotoxicity or proliferation, revealing relationships between BATF2, JUN-, and CREB1-family bZIPs. Using a combination of epistasis, transcriptome, proteome, and AP-MS interactome analyses of BATF2 and AEL-CREM, we discovered functional overlap in their inhibition of pro-dysfunction CREB1-family activity, potentially driven by unexpected binding of CREB1-family members by overexpressed BATF2. Their function diverged in BATF2's early promotion of pro-proliferation AP-1 activity and later physical and functional interactions with BACH2, contributing to persistence. These findings were mirrored in murine chronic viral infection and syngeneic tumor models, where BATF2 or AEL-CREM overexpression were notably pro-proliferative and anti-exhaustion. Together, these results illuminate new connections and functional roles enabled by bZIP family perturbations, with implications for modulating T-cell state.

papers.title: A synthetic phageome reveals widespread and diverse human antibody responses to bacteriophages
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages colonize humans, yet their recognition by humoral immunity remains unclear. We developed PhageScan, a PhIP- Seq platform comprising 277,051 phage and 49,630 human viral oligopeptides. Profiling sera from 192 healthy donors without prior phage therapy characterized anti-phage response specificity and revealed widespread, strong IgG reactivity to phages, comparable in prevalence and magnitude to that against human viruses. Recognition patterns were however highly individualized. Among phage sequences, 12,576 peptides were significantly enriched in at least two individuals. Strongly immunogenic epitopes preferentially originated from phages infecting pathogenic bacteria, whereas widely shared ''public'' epitopes were enriched among phages of environmental and food-associated bacteria. ImmE, a lactococcal phage endolysin recognized in 59.9% of individuals, showed reduced antibacterial activity in the presence of sera identified as ImmE-reactive by PhageScan, demonstrating functional relevance. These findings establish phage-directed antibodies as a widespread component of human immunity and PhageScan as a scalable platform for defining phage--antibody interactions.

papers.title: Follistatin-like 1 Promotes Neutrophil-mediated Host Defense against Klebsiella pneumoniae
papers.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of pneumonia and highly burdensome etiology of antibiotic-resistant infections constituting an urgent public health threat. Follistatin-like 1 (FSTL-1) is implicated in many processes including lung development and homeostasis, tissue remodeling, and inflammation though its role in antibacterial immunity remains poorly defined. We have observed that FSTL-1 is elevated in the lungs of both humans and mice during bacterial pneumonia. Using an inducible Fstl1 knockout mouse model, we demonstrate that FSTL-1 is required for pulmonary bacterial clearance and neutrophil recruitment during K. pneumoniae infection. Recombinant FSTL-1 rescues Fstl1-deficient susceptibility and enhances clearance of K. pneumoniae in wild-type mice. Mechanistically, FSTL-1-mediated protection was lost upon neutrophil depletion and in Cd14-deficient or Nr4a1 deficient mice, components of a lung-specific neutrophil transcriptional program. These findings identify FSTL-1 as a lung-derived factor that licenses neutrophil-mediated antibacterial defense via a novel FSTL-1/CD14/NR4A1-dependent signaling pathway critical for protection against bacterial pneumonia.

papers.title: Ascorbate and TET2 couple balanced hematopoiesis to disease tolerance
papers.abstract: Infections stimulate myelopoiesis but this comes at the cost of reduced production of other lineages. It is unclear if this imbalance is protective or damaging, and if factors that promote balanced hematopoiesis can impact infection pathology. Here we show that the ascorbate-TET axis limits excessive myelopoiesis, promotes balanced hematopoiesis, and is essential for surviving malaria. Hematopoietic-specific ascorbate depletion promoted myelopoiesis. The effects of ascorbate were mediated by TET2/TET3 activity in myeloid progenitors. Combined ascorbate and TET2 depletion markedly skewed hematopoiesis to the myeloid lineage and impaired erythropoiesis. Ascorbate is commonly depleted in infections, but the functional significance of this remains unclear. In the absence of ascorbate and TET2, mice infected with Plasmodium parasites could clear the pathogen, but had exacerbated myeloid and impaired erythroid response, anemia, and tissue damage and they succumbed to infection, indicating compromised disease tolerance. Therefore ascorbate and TET2 promote balanced hematopoiesis to impart tolerance to malaria.
